channel.title: Kelvin
channel.description: Updates for Kelvin, the local-AI photo editor for macOS.

item.title: Kelvin 0.7.0 — hold the answers against each other
item.description:
Kelvin 0.7.0

You can hold Kelvin’s answers against each other now — and three things that were wrong in 0.6.0 are named below rather than buried.

See the choice you are being asked to make

Kelvin offers you several finished interpretations of a photograph and asks you to pick one. Until now it asked you to make that choice from four thumbnails the size of a postage stamp and a line of numbers like “+18 contrast”. That is a fair question to put to somebody who can read those numbers and picture the result. It is not a fair question to put to anybody else.

Press C, or the new Compare button, and the candidates take over the canvas at full size. Two at a time by default, or all four when you want the survey. Click the photograph you prefer and that is your pick; 1–4 choose, C or Esc closes.

Zoom and pan apply to every tile at once — two crops of different parts of the frame are not a comparison of two edits. And the tiles are re-rendered at canvas resolution rather than scaled up from the thumbnails, because a comparison of anything other than what you would actually get is worse than no comparison.

The colour grade was wrong, and is now right

Every look that grades colour — Vivid, Dramatic, Warm, Rich, Teal & orange — applied its grade through the wrong gamma. It came out weak in the highlights and pointed the wrong way in the shadows: a look asking for cool shadows produced a warm cast instead.

Measured against 77 photographs with the photographer’s own finished edit as the reference, every graded look moved closer to what the photographer actually did — Soft 7.77 → 7.72, Rich 9.63 → 9.48, Vivid 10.29 → 10.08, Dramatic 10.76 → 10.52, Warm 10.05 → 9.79.

The look a photograph opens in is unchanged — Natural measures identically before and after. This moves the looks you reach for when Natural is not what you wanted.

An edit could be deleted, and no longer can

This is the one worth reading. If you clicked a third thumbnail while the second photograph was still decoding, Kelvin could file an empty editing panel under the photograph you had just left — and because an empty panel looks like an unedited one, it then removed that photograph’s saved edit from disk. A brush mask, a look, a set of retouched spots: gone.

It is fixed and pinned by tests. If you have lost work this way, this release cannot bring it back; nothing wrote it anywhere else.

“Include location” off now really means off

0.6.0 said that turning location off stripped everything identifying from a shared photograph. That was not completely true. Cameras that write the extended Exif block — many Sony, Canon and Nikon bodies — still carried the camera body’s serial number and the owner name recorded in the camera, and place names written by other software survived as well. A serial number is a tracking key: the same body in two shared photographs links them to one person.

All of it is removed now. If you shared photographs from 0.6.0 with location turned off, those files still contain those fields.

Also fixed

  • A colour-based mask (Skin, or a colour range) silently stopped working the moment a black-and-white look was applied — it selected nothing at all, with no error.
  • Contrast through a Background mask pivoted on the brightness of the subject instead of the background it was adjusting.
  • Exposure fusion and the clarity controls faded out in a band around the edge of the frame, more so at export size than in the preview.
  • Exporting as HEIC or 16-bit TIFF wrote those bytes into a file the save panel had renamed .jpeg.
  • The Temp slider showed “as shot” as 5500 K when the neutral is 6500 K, so the first small drag jumped the photograph about 1000 K warmer.
  • Pressing Apply and then touching the filmstrip cancelled the whole-shoot scene read outright, and nothing restarted it.
  • Reopening a photograph from another folder left the filmstrip listing the folder you had left, with that folder’s look and export label still attached.

What still does not work

Kelvin does not learn from which candidate you pick. The pick is recorded; nothing reads it. A toned black-and-white look (Selenium) renders silvery rather than toned, and several looks declare a warmth shift that has no effect on most photographs. A batch export cannot be cancelled once it is running. The canvas is softer than the exported file — export and open at 100% to judge sharpness.

Everything runs on your Mac. No account, no upload, and nothing leaves the machine except this update check — which you can switch off in Settings. Sharing a photo sends it where you send it, with location stripped unless you tick the box.

item.title: Kelvin 0.6.0 — it reads ahead of you, and it learned to share
item.description:
Kelvin 0.6.0

Kelvin reads ahead of you now, and it learned to share.

Send a photo from your Mac

A Share button sits next to Export. It renders the photo you are looking at through the exact pipeline Export uses, then hands the file to Messages, AirDrop or Mail. Location is stripped by default — texting someone a photo should not text them where your house is. When the frame carries a GPS position, an “Include location” checkbox appears beside the button, so including it is a choice you make each time, never a setting that silently remembers.

The scene reading works ahead of your browsing

Whenever you open a photo, Kelvin quietly reads the sixteen frames around it, in the order you are most likely to reach them — so arrowing through a shoot increasingly lands on frames whose reading is already done. Your click still comes first: opening a photo cancels the background read mid-thought and starts yours immediately.

Sixteen is deliberate. Browsing should not commit your laptop’s GPU to a four-hundred-frame folder you opened by accident; “Apply to shoot” still reads everything, and now says how long it will take.

Time remaining, where waiting happens

The folder scan and batch export now say “about 4 minutes left” — coarsely on purpose, so the number never jitters like a countdown. And reopening a shoot you have scanned before is no longer minutes: measurements are kept on disk, so the Best, Focus and Flagged filters come back in about a second on a folder measured once.

The model can name what it sees

The scene line now says what the subject is in plain words — “sea stack”, “starfish”, “bride” — and a landscape with one dominant natural feature finally counts as having a subject at all. Kelvin could describe a frame as “dark silhouette of sea stacks” and still report nothing to edit; now the sea stacks get the same corrective attention a backlit face would.

The names are the model’s own words, and they are display-only — no edit is ever decided by free text.

Fixed

  • Renaming a mask in the same moment it was deleted could crash the app. It no longer can.
  • A large batch export grew its memory without bound — about 60 GB over a 400-frame RAW shoot. It now stays flat near 5 GB and finishes sooner.
  • The folder scan re-sorted the whole shoot once per frame; big folders no longer make the window feel thick while scanning.

One honest cost

The scene reading’s vocabulary changed, so readings cached by earlier versions answer a question Kelvin no longer asks. The first time you open an already-read shoot, Kelvin re-reads those scenes once, in the background. Your edits are untouched.

What still does not work

Healing is place-and-delete. You can add a patch, remove it or undo it — you cannot drag or resize one after the fact. A heal into busy texture blends rather than refuses; look at it at 100%. The canvas is softer than the exported file — export and open at 100% to judge sharpness. The wand walks into anything touching its target that is the same colour; the brush’s Erase mode takes the spill back off. Deliberately dark photographs get lifted; turn Exposure back down.

Everything runs on your Mac. No account, no upload, and nothing leaves the machine except this update check — which you can switch off in Settings. Sharing a photo sends it where you send it, with location stripped unless you tick the box.

item.title: Kelvin 0.5.0 — point at the blemish, and colour that leaves the light alone
item.description:
Kelvin 0.5.0

A heal tool you aim yourself, and white balance that corrects the light instead of the picture.

A heal tool, in place of a detector that found sand

0.4.0’s notes said it plainly: dust detection finds sand, not dust. This release stops trying.

It was measured before it was deleted. Four frames from one shoot, same camera, same f/11, taken minutes apart, returned 0, 0, 1 and 40 spots. Dust sits at a fixed place on the sensor and lands in the same spot in every frame — real dust would have given nearly the same list four times. That spread is proof it was finding scene content.

So finding the blemish goes back to you, which is the part you were always better at. Press H, click the speck, and Kelvin patches it from a clean piece of the same photograph. [ and ] resize, ⌥-click removes a patch, ⌘Z undoes.

Patches are stored as a position and a radius rather than as pixels, so one click survives a full-resolution export and travels to the rest of the shoot.

White balance corrects the light, not the picture

On a finished frame of blue water under a blue sky, Kelvin applied a 3920 K warm shift and turned the sky beige. It had seen a blue scene and corrected the blue out of it.

Averaging the whole frame cannot tell the light was yellow from the picture is mostly sea. Kelvin now reads the least chromatic parts of the frame to decide whether there is a cast, and local colour differences to decide how much to take out.

Across 47 finished photographs, the share correctly left alone went from 23% to 81% — and casts are now fully removed rather than half removed.

Whites stop asking for everything

Kelvin aimed every frame’s white point at 0.965. Over 38 finished photographs, exactly one reached it — so the rule handed out its maximum lift on 25 of them and could not tell a frame needing a little from one needing a lot. The target is now 0.88, where real finished work actually sits.

What still does not work

Healing is place-and-delete. You can add a patch, remove it or undo it — you cannot drag or resize one after the fact. A heal into busy texture blends rather than refuses: Kelvin always patches where you click, even where nothing nearby matches well, so on detailed ground the patch can be visible at 100%. The canvas is softer than the exported file — it draws a scaled-up preview rather than re-rendering at the size you are looking at. Deliberately dark photographs get lifted; turn Exposure back down.

Everything runs on your Mac. No account, no upload, and nothing leaves the machine except this update check — which you can switch off in Settings.

item.title: Kelvin 0.4.0 — quicker to open, truer to the photograph
item.description:
Kelvin 0.4.0

Quicker to open, and truer to the photograph in front of it.

A natural edit is natural again

Kelvin's first candidate is called Natural, and on a grey coastal frame it was brightening the sky, opening the shadows, and putting an S-curve and a colour grade over the top. Its own reading of that photograph was “dark silhouette of large sea stacks against a gloomy sky” — so it saw the weather correctly and then removed it.

The line is now drawn where a photographer would draw it. Exposure, white balance, highlight and shadow recovery and dehaze are fixes — nobody looks at a corrected exposure and calls it a look. An S-curve with a split-tone grade, a 52-point spread between the black and white points, and half-strength exposure fusion are a look, and a flat scene photographed flat is allowed to stay flat.

On that frame: whites +28 → +11, blacks −24 → −10, fusion 55 → 20, and no curve at all. The punch is not gone — it is what Vivid and Dramatic are for, one click away.

The white line around the rock

A backlit subject gets lifted out of shadow, and the mask that lift travels through comes from Vision. When Vision finds no person it falls back to whatever stands out most — which, on a landscape, is the landscape. Kelvin had correctly read walkers on the sand, believed the mask was those people, and lifted a sea stack instead. The lift met the rock's soft edge against a bright sky and drew a rim around it.

A mask now carries where it came from, and a person lift requires a mask that actually found a person. Animals still use the fallback deliberately — person segmentation never fires for a dog. The manual Subject pop control no longer claims “the detected person” over a rock either; it says what was really found.

A shoot on a network drive opens

Opening a folder on a sleeping NAS froze the window before a single byte was read — the file-system checks and the date-reading pass were running on the thread that draws the interface, so Kelvin sat waiting on the mount with nothing on screen. All of that moved off it.

Thumbnails, capture dates and content fingerprints are also remembered between launches. On a 126-frame shoot from a local SSD — the conservative case, with no slow network involved — reading capture dates went from 820 ms to 13 ms and building the filmstrip from 637 ms to 7 ms.

That cache is half a megabyte, it lives in ~/Library/Caches, and it is safe to delete — everything in it rebuilds from your photographs in milliseconds.

Candidates in a third of the time

Composing the looks for a 60-megapixel raw file took 189–263 ms and now takes 65–74 ms. Eight candidates are eight gradings of one photograph, so Kelvin was finding the same faces eight times over; detection now runs once for the set, while the measurement of what each grade did to skin still happens per candidate, because that is the part that has to differ.

The small image the scene reading uses is also derived from one Kelvin already has, rather than built again from the raw file — which used to cost most of a second. Checked across 79 real frames: 78 produced an identical edit, and the exception differed by a hundredth of a stop.

The panel

  • It resizes, by dragging its inner edge, and remembers the width next time.
  • The divider follows the pointer instead of drifting away from it mid-drag.
  • It comes off entirely when you want the photograph and nothing else.

Smaller things

  • Kelvin can offer to become your default photo app — once, at the moment a photograph is on screen with its candidates up, so you can see what a double-click would get you first.
  • A hairline of light along the top of the window, warm through daylight to cool: the same blackbody ramp the temperature slider is built from.

What still does not work

Dust detection finds sand, not dust. It reports scene texture and patches about 120 pixels out of a million, which is why the toggle looks like it does nothing. Heal spots placed by hand do work. The canvas is softer than the exported file — it draws a scaled-up preview rather than re-rendering at the size you are looking at, so the exported file has detail the screen does not show; open it at 100% to judge sharpness.

Everything runs on your Mac. No account, no upload, and nothing leaves the machine except this update check — which you can switch off in Settings.

item.title: Kelvin 0.3.0 — point at the thing you want to edit
item.description:
Kelvin 0.3.0

Point at the thing you want to edit — and take it back off again.

Select anything, not just what Kelvin recognises

Subject detection finds whatever stands out most and stops. On a coastal frame that means it hands back the big sea stack and neither of the two smaller ones beside it. Those had nothing to click.

The wand fills that gap. Click the thing you want and the selection spreads from there until the picture stops matching, staying inside whatever you pointed at. It is stored as the point you clicked plus a tolerance — never as pixels — so the region is regrown at whatever size is being rendered. The selection you approve on screen is the one that reaches a full-resolution export.

It will not do everything. Where the thing you clicked touches something else the same colour, the fill walks straight into it. No tolerance fixes that, because the path between them really is the same colour. Kelvin says so when it happens, and the brush below is how you fix it.

The brush can subtract

Every mask was built by adding, so one that grabbed too much had to be deleted and drawn again. The brush now has Add and Erase. Paint over the rock, switch to Erase, take the spill back off the sky.

A soft brush erases softly — the edge is scaled rather than cut, so taking part of a feathered mask away does not leave a hard-edged hole in it.

Best actually filters now

Best shows one frame per group of alike ones, the sharpest of each. It was reading measurements that nothing ever started, so on a shoot you had not separately scanned it returned everything, and waiting did not help. Choosing it now asks for the measurement it needs — as do Focus and Flagged — and opening a different shoot measures that one too.

On a 437-frame shoot that is 148 groups: two thirds of it collapses.

Export says what it will do

  • The size button no longer lies. It read “Export full-res” while honouring a size you chose once and forgot. It now names the size it will write.
  • The group button names a scope, not a bare number, and counts what will really be written.
  • A selection is the scope. Export was the one action that ignored selected frames. Select four and it exports four.
  • Filename prefix and suffix are remembered, alongside the naming scheme — and the panel no longer disagrees with itself about the name it is about to use.

Everything runs on your Mac. No account, no upload, and nothing leaves the machine except this update check — which you can switch off in Settings.

item.title: Kelvin 0.2.0 — updates are 1.4 MB, and the panel keeps up
